analysis.one_liner: Restores the consumer finance watchdog's enforcement powers, bans forced arbitration clauses, and gives consumers free credit scores.
analysis.headline: The House passed the Consumers First Act 231-191 on May 22, 2019, with every voting Democrat in favor and every voting Republican opposed, but it died in the Senate Banking Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau — the federal agency that polices mortgages, credit cards, debt collectors, and payday lenders — to keep its enforcement offices staffed and active, and to publish consumer complaints publicly. It would reinstate a rule letting customers sue financial companies in class actions instead of being forced into private arbitration, require credit bureaus to give consumers a free credit score each year, and limit debt collectors to unlimited automated texts. The House passed it in May 2019; the Senate never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who deal with banks, credit card companies, debt collectors, payday and car-title lenders, credit bureaus, and student loan servicers. The bill would let customers band together in class action lawsuits rather than be forced into individual arbitration, give everyone one free credit score a year from each major credit bureau, restore the CFPB's fair-lending and student loan oversight offices, require public reporting on payday lender fees and repo rates, and stop debt collectors from unlimited automated texting.

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the CFPB arbitration rule, which bars financial companies from using fine-print clauses to block customers from joining class action lawsuits [S4, S5].
Requires nationwide credit bureaus to provide a free credit score with the free annual credit report they already must provide [S4, S5].

Requires the CFPB to publish all consumer complaints in a searchable public database and stops the Director from shrinking or renaming its enforcement offices, including the Office of Fair Lending and Equal Opportunity [S2, S4].

Restores CFPB information-sharing agreements with the Department of Education for overseeing federal student loans, and recreates the Office of Students and Young Consumers with an annual public report on risks to student borrowers [S4, S5].

Requires quarterly reports on debt collection complaints, payday loan and car-title loan enforcement, estimated payday fees and repossession rates, and an annual report on complaints from consumers 62 and older [S4, S5].
Bars the CFPB Director from issuing a debt collection rule allowing unlimited email and text messages to consumers, and blocks new exemptions from Home Mortgage Disclosure Act reporting [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Financial companies that would face the costs: banks and consumer lenders that could no longer use arbitration clauses to avoid class actions, credit bureaus that must supply free scores, debt collectors limited in how they can contact people, payday and car-title lenders facing closer scrutiny and public reporting, student loan servicers required to file annual data reports, and smaller lenders that would lose exemptions from mortgage disclosure reporting.

drawbacks.text: Financial industry opponents argued the arbitration rule benefits class-action lawyers while giving customers who join class actions smaller individual recoveries than arbitration can provide, and raises costs that lenders may pass on to borrowers [S8 — Republicans backed a motion to recommit limiting Civil Penalty Fund spending on this ground].

The bill lowers the mortgage disclosure exemption threshold, so institutions originating fewer than 500 loans would face full Home Mortgage Disclosure Act reporting for the first time — a real compliance cost for small banks and credit unions [S4, S5].

The bill dictates the agency's internal structure in statute — staffing levels, political appointee counts, office names, even in-person advisory board meetings — which reduces the Director's ability to manage the agency and locks in organizational choices that future Congresses would have to revisit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefits are concrete and directly tied to the bill's core purpose: class action rights, free credit scores, and an empowered enforcement agency. The main costs fall on regulated financial firms, plus compliance burdens on small lenders. The biggest good-faith objection — that class actions favor lawyers over individual plaintiffs — is genuine but concerns the pre-existing arbitration rule the bill simply restores. On balance this is a consumer-protection bill whose costs land mainly on the industry it would regulate.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill in May 2019, but it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never brought it to a vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The House Financial Services Committee reported the bill on May 10, 2019, by a 34-26 vote, and the House passed it 231-191 on May 22, 2019 [S7].
The vote was entirely on party lines: 231 of 234 voting Democrats voted yes and 0 voted no; 0 of 197 voting Republicans voted yes and 191 voted no [S8 roll 228].

Republicans' final attempt — a motion to send the bill back with instructions restricting use of the CFPB's Civil Penalty Fund — failed 191-231, again with all Republicans in favor and all Democrats opposed [S7, roll 227].
The Senate received the bill on May 23, 2019, and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, where no further action was taken [S1, S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks, payday and car-title lenders, debt collectors, credit bureaus, and student loan servicers are better off because the bill died: none of the arbitration, free-credit-score, or enforcement-oversight requirements took effect, and the Trump-era CFPB structure the bill targeted remained in place through the end of the 116th Congress.

for.name: Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, guided it through committee markup (reported 34-26), and managed its passage on the House floor.

for.name: 231 of 234 voting House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously to pass the bill on final passage (roll call 228) and unanimously against the motion to recommit (roll call 227).

for.name: 29 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 23, 2019, and never held a markup or brought it to the Senate floor, where it died.

against.name: 191 of 197 voting House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted unanimously against final passage and unanimously for the motion to recommit with instructions on the Civil Penalty Fund.

against.name: Financial services industry
against.role: Regulated banks, payday lenders, debt collectors, and credit bureaus
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill's arbitration reinstatement and expanded reporting requirements; the House-passed bill's core provisions would reverse industry-backed actions, including the 2017 repeal of the arbitration rule.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split cleanly by party: 231-191 for passage with zero Democrats voting no and zero Republicans voting yes, and the same 191-231 split on the motion to recommit.

industries.note: The bill reinstates the arbitration rule, forcing lenders to face class actions instead of routing disputes into individual arbitration, and blocks new exemptions from mortgage disclosure reporting. Banks' savings from avoiding class litigation come at consumers' expense.

Quarterly public reports would expose payday fees, rollover rates, and car repossessions, and the bill's findings fault the agency for dropping payday lender enforcement. Their fee revenue depends on practices the bill targets for scrutiny.
The bill bars a debt collection rule allowing unlimited consumer emails and texts and requires quarterly reporting on complaints and enforcement actions against collectors.
The three nationwide bureaus would have to furnish a free credit score with each free annual disclosure, giving away a score they currently sell.
Servicers would file annual reports on portfolios, borrower contacts, and income-driven repayment applications, under a restored CFPB-Department of Education oversight partnership.

They lose the exemption from certain mortgage disclosure requirements, gaining real reporting costs, though the bill also seeks community bank and credit union representation on the CFPB's advisory board.
